content.p: The Catholic diocese of Maitland-Newcastle serves the Hunter region of New South Wales. For most of its history it was known only as a regional church, with a cathedral, parishes and Catholic schools. Since the 1990s it has become known in Australia for something else: a cluster of convicted priests and brothers, decades of complaints that were not passed to police, and two of the country's major inquiries. A survivor of abuse by one of its priests, Peter Gogarty, called the Hunter a kind of "epicentre" for abuse within the Catholic Church. A representative of the advocacy group Broken Rites said the pattern was found elsewhere in Australia too, and that Newcastle and Ballarat had simply become notorious.

The diocese told the Royal Commission in 2016 that it had substantiated 158 claims involving 31 perpetrators. Over the years its leaders have been criticised, and in two cases prosecuted, for how they handled what they knew. One of those prosecutions ended with the conviction of an archbishop in 2018, which was overturned on appeal months later.

Before 1866 the Hunter was served by priests sent up from Sydney. A papal brief of 27 May 1847 created a Diocese of Maitland, but its first nominated bishop, Charles Henry Davis, stayed in Sydney and died in 1854 without taking possession. James Murray was nominated in 1865 and took possession on 1 November 1866, making West Maitland's St John the Baptist Church his cathedral. Over the next century the boundaries moved several times. A papal brief of 14 June 1995 renamed it the Diocese of Maitland-Newcastle, and Sacred Heart Church in Hamilton became its cathedral the following month, according to the diocese's own history.
The year 1995 matters for another reason. It was the year police charged the diocese's most notorious priest.
content.h2: Vincent Ryan and what the monsignor knew
content.p: Vincent Ryan was ordained in Rome in 1966 by Pope Paul VI. In the Hunter he worked in a string of parishes, and his later victims included altar boys. The Newcastle Herald, which reconstructed the case in 2007 from police documents, set out a timeline. In 1974 a mother reported to Monsignor Patrick Cotter, who was then running the diocese as acting bishop, that Ryan had indecently assaulted two boys aged six and eight. In December 1975 Cotter was told of more serious assaults, and Ryan admitted them. Ryan was sent to Melbourne for a year, which Ryan later described as a "cover-up", the paper reported.

Cotter's own letters survive. Writing in December 1975 to a priest-psychiatrist, he said the problem had become known to him about a year earlier, and called his handling of it "a mistake on my part". Bishop Leo Clarke took over the diocese in June 1976. In 1977 Ryan returned and resumed offending against boys aged six to 14, and was moved from parish to parish until 1991, the Herald reported. Its account includes a woman who in 1990 told a diocesan priest that Ryan was still offending and said the priest walked away, and a mother who phoned Cotter in May 1991 and was told "We'll deal with it". Nothing happened.

Police investigated in 1995 and Ryan was charged in October. In 1996 and 1997 he pleaded guilty to two rounds of offences, and the Herald reported a total sentence of 16 years for more than 50 charges involving 26 victims aged six to 14. Later ABC reporting gave different totals, describing a 14-year sentence for abusing 34 boys between 1973 and 1991. Ryan appealed his sentence in 2002 and lost.

Police also looked at the people above him. In January 1996 they interviewed Cotter, then 82, about whether he had concealed a serious crime and forwarded a brief to the Director of Public Prosecutions that recommended a prosecution. The Canberra Times later reported that the Director declined, in part because of Cotter's age. Bishop Clarke was interviewed in July 1996; he denied knowing of Ryan's activities but admitted reinstating him. Cotter died in August 2007, and Bishop Michael Malone conducted his funeral.

Ryan returned to court. In 2019 a District Court judge found him guilty of abusing two more altar boys at Hunter parishes in the 1970s and 1990s and gave him up to three years and three months in jail. Ryan, who had been released in 2010, was by then 81. In an ABC interview broadcast in 2020 he said he had confessed his offending to a priest and had been told he would go to jail if he did not stop, and that he felt "momentarily" free after absolution. When he was arrested in 1995 the church withdrew his faculties, but he remained a priest, and Bishop Bill Wright said he had written to the Vatican about Ryan's status.

Two other priests shaped the later inquiries. James Fletcher was charged in 2004 with child sex abuse crimes, was convicted, and died in prison in early 2006. Denis McAlinden arrived in the Hunter from Ireland in 1949. He was charged in Western Australia in 1992 with abuse of a girl and acquitted, and he died there in 2005 without facing charges for his conduct in the Hunter.

In 2012 a police officer, Peter Fox, told the ABC's Lateline program that the area had seen a cover-up of child sex offences. His words were: "There's something very wrong when you have so many paedophile priests operating in such a small area for such an extended period of time with immunity." The New South Wales government set up a Special Commission of Inquiry under Margaret Cunneen SC. At its 2013 hearings counsel told the inquiry that the church had had "extensive knowledge dating back to the 1950s" of McAlinden's abuse. Letters read to the hearing showed that in 1976 officials described the allegations as "not extremely serious" and recommended he move to a Western Australian diocese, with one letter saying this would give "a good cover-up for his resigning the parish". Bishop Wright apologised from the witness stand, describing McAlinden and Fletcher as "sexual predators".

Cunneen reported in 2014, releasing three of four volumes. The ABC summarised her conclusions this way: the inquiry cast doubt over Fox's claims of a police cover-up, but found that church officials had known of allegations against priests for decades and failed to act. The fourth volume, which contained findings that could bear on criminal charges, was held back and not released until September 2019.

The Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse held its 43rd public hearing in Newcastle from 31 August 2016. Counsel assisting, Stephen Free, opened by telling it that there was "a long and disturbing history of suffering by children" in the diocese inflicted by diocesan priests and members of religious orders. By his account the diocese had substantiated claims from 158 people against 31 perpetrators, about 56 per cent of the claims involved priests, and the diocese had paid 46 claimants from one school alone, St Pius X in Adamstown. The Herald reported the total paid as more than $25.7 million, including $2.9 million to one Ryan victim.

The commission examined the handling of Ryan and the Marist Brothers' response to three of their members: Francis Cable (Brother Romuald), Thomas Butler (Brother Patrick) and Darcy O'Sullivan (Brother Dominic). Gerard McDonald, who was an altar boy with Ryan, told it he had dreaded the moment Ryan took off his glasses. Two nuns who learned of the abuse in the 1970s, including one who gave evidence as a psychologist, said they had not thought it was a crime; under questioning by the chair, Justice Peter McClellan, one agreed that if she had treated it as a crime Ryan would have been dealt with by the law far sooner.

Bishop Malone, the diocese's former bishop, conceded under questioning from McClellan that the church had engaged in a cover-up, the Newcastle Herald editorial said, though it noted he had also done much behind the scenes to push the church in the right direction. The head of the Marist Brothers, Brother Peter Carroll, apologised to the family of Andrew Nash, 13, who took his own life in 1974, and told the commission the order had failed to act on the crimes and excessive violence of many of its Brothers.

Bishop Wright gave a statement of acknowledgement. He said Ryan "was a sexual predator who used his status as a priest" and that Cotter "abjectly failed" to protect children after being told in 1974. He said Bishop Clarke might have known of Ryan's abuse, and that attitudes in the diocese which put "the perceived good of the Church before the safety of a child" were fundamental to Ryan's ability to keep offending for over 20 years. He apologised unreservedly on behalf of the diocese.

The Hunter also produced concealment prosecutions, and the Newcastle Herald counted such cases against church leaders as very few worldwide. The Herald reported that a senior diocesan priest, whom it described as Malone's "right-hand man", was convicted in 2009 of making a false statement to police about a priest who could not be named for legal reasons.

The better-known case was that of Philip Wilson, later Archbishop of Adelaide and in 1976 a priest of the Maitland diocese. Police charged him in March 2015 with concealing Fletcher's abuse. The prosecution case, as the Guardian summarised it, was that two altar boys told him in 1976 of Fletcher's abuse and that he did nothing. The main witness, Peter Creigh, said he went to Wilson twice. In May 2018 Newcastle magistrate Robert Stone convicted him, and on 3 July sentenced him to 12 months, saying his primary motive had been to protect the Catholic Church. Home detention followed in August. Wilson resigned as archbishop in July.

On 6 December 2018 District Court Judge Roy Ellis quashed the conviction. He found Wilson an honest witness and said the Crown had not proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. Ellis accepted that Creigh was honest, but questioned the reliability of his memory after so many years, citing evidence from a memory expert, and listed 12 inconsistencies in Creigh's accounts. Those inconsistencies, he said, did not prove the conversation never happened but could raise reasonable doubt. The judge also dismissed a prosecution appeal against the leniency of the sentence.

The fourth volume of the Cunneen report came out in September 2019. It found Wilson "an unsatisfactory and unimpressive witness" who had given evidence the commission considered untruthful, and it said he should have reported McAlinden to police. It described Wilson's evidence about forgetting his 1987 contacts over McAlinden as "improbable". It found that Malone had deliberately failed to tell police in 2011 of Creigh, whom he had met in 2010, and called some of his evidence "unsatisfactory and untruthful in certain respects". Peter Gogarty said it showed Creigh was credible. These were findings of a commission of inquiry, made in a separate process from the criminal appeal, which had acquitted Wilson.

In the Marist Brothers' case, William Wade, known as Brother Christopher, a former principal of the Hamilton school, pleaded guilty in February 2020 to two counts of failing to give police information during investigations into Cable and O'Sullivan. The Herald called it the first such guilty plea by a senior member of a religious order in Australia. Wade had been jailed for at least 18 months in 2017 for indecently assaulting two boys. In September 2020 Acting Judge Michael Adams gave him a four-month sentence served as a community corrections order, saying his inaction and silence contributed to terrible consequences but that he could only be punished for the offences before the court. Geoffrey Nash, whose brother Andrew died in 1974, said Wade should apologise to their mother.

In 2018 Wright wrote a letter acknowledging Father Tom Brennan, principal of St Pius X College from 1973 to 1983, as a child sex offender, after the diocese settled a claim by the barrister James Miller. Brennan had died in 2012 while facing charges concerning two other former students.

In October 2025 the Newcastle Herald reported that survivors and their lawyers said the church had become harder to deal with. Solicitor Robert McKessar said the church and Marist Brothers were taking "a much tougher line" than before, and that the average payment through the national redress scheme was about $90,000, compared with hundreds of thousands of dollars for a significant civil claim. The diocese said it knew of no change in how fast negotiations or litigation were moving, that each claim was considered on its merits, and that it remained deeply sorry for the harm caused. Survivors Geoffrey Nash and Stephen Murray said a memorial promised after the Royal Commission had not been built at the schools concerned.
